note: Absolute ceilings for the headline metrics, enforced by compare.py
(--budgets) on top of the relative gate.  The relative gate alone cannot
stop slow drift: it compares HEAD against the latest tag only, and seven
release hops in five days at the maximum legal 15% each is 2.7x slower
with a green gate every time.  A breach fails the release even when the
relative gate passes, and [perf:accept] does not excuse it.
Bump ritual: raising a ceiling is a deliberate, reviewed edit to this
file, made in the same PR as the change that needs it, with the commit
message saying why the new ceiling is acceptable.  Update 'observed'
(the merged best-of-rounds CI value the ceiling was sized against) and
'set' when you do.  Ceilings sit well above observed values (roughly
+60%) because ubuntu-latest runners vary run to run; the relative gate
handles single-release moves, this file only caps the compounding.
LOWERING a ceiling is the same edit and needs doing more often than
raising one.  A ceiling is sized against the metric of its day, so every
optimization that lands leaves its own ceiling too loose, silently, and
a drift cap at 5x the real value caps nothing.  Eight of the nine below
were re-stamped on 2026-08-07 from CI run 31170258121 for exactly that
reason (config.parse_yaml_3k already carried a value from that run).
The stamps they replaced ran from 1.37x to 5.35x of the measured value:
schedule.cold_build_100k read 2.586 against a real 0.483, so its 4.0
ceiling was sitting at 8.3x.  Re-stamp the whole file whenever a release
lands a broad optimization, not only the entries that failed.
Values are the metric's own unit: seconds, except mem.* in MB.  Time
budgets compare the RAW measured value, NOT the startup.python_baseline
subtraction the relative gate applies, so a startup.* ceiling has to
leave room for the interpreter's own ~18 ms.
'proposed' below is NOT read by compare.py (it loads 'budgets' only).
It is where a ceiling waits out the ritual: a metric added this cycle
has no merged best-of-rounds CI value to size a ceiling against, and
an ubuntu-latest number is not a local one.  Move an entry into
'budgets' once one release has published an 'observed' value for it,
filling in 'observed' and 'set' at the same time.
Promoting an entry means RE-SIZING 'max' from that observed value, not
just adding the field.  The 'local' figures recorded below are developer
machine measurements and every proposed 'max' was derived from one at
~1.7x, which is what produced the parse_yaml_3k false red described
further down.  There is no sound machine-wide conversion factor to
reuse instead: the runner came in at 1.84x local on parse_yaml_3k and
0.94x local on startup.import_daemon, and these five span Chromium
rendering, asyncio timer scheduling and GC pauses.  A 'local' number
shows the metric is worth capping.  Size the cap from CI.
config.parse_yaml_3k was armed one release ahead of the ritual because
it exists for more than drift: it catches a return of the quadratic Seq
validation that config._patch_strictyaml_seq_deepcopy hoists out of the
element loop.  A re-vendor of upstream strictyaml plus a trusting
[perf:accept] would otherwise ship the quadratic parse with every gate
green.  Arming it early cost one false red: the first ceiling was 2.0s,
sized as ~1.7x a 1.176s local figure, and the first CI comparison came
in at 2.164s, so the ceiling sat UNDER the metric rather than over it.
That same comparison measured the thing the ceiling exists to catch,
because the 1.2.36 side of it still had the quadratic parse: 11.025s,
on the same runner in the same weather.  So 3.5s sits 1.6x above the
linear parse and 3.1x below the quadratic one, and a reintroduction
still fires even if the relative gate is waived.  Raising it past ~7s
gives that up, so say why in the commit message if you ever do.
config.parse_yaml_300 covers the far more common config size and its old
0.381 stamp predated the hoist, so 0.216 is the post-hoist value.  Do not
read that as a second anti-quadratic net: at 300 jobs the slip is only a
1.376x bulge (bench.py records 0.161s against 0.117s and calls the signal
almost absent at that size), so a reintroduced quadratic parse lands near
0.297s and passes the 0.35 ceiling.  Breaching it would take a 1.62x
bulge.  The re-stamp buys parse_yaml_300 a working DRIFT cap and nothing
more; parse_yaml_3k is the only entry that catches the quadratic parse.
startup.import_daemon and mem.rss_daemon_import carried stamps taken on
2026-07-25, roughly 18 hours BEFORE cron.py's lazy aiohttp door landed,
so both described a tree that imported the whole web stack eagerly.
Their observed values are now the door-closed ones, and the two ceilings
behave differently against a reopened door, which measured 0.323s and
49.1MB.  startup.import_daemon at 0.30 DOES fire on it: that regression
is +80% against a +68% ceiling.  Do not loosen that one casually, it is
the tightest absolute gate on the door anywhere in the repo.
mem.rss_daemon_import at 57.0 does not, because +61% of headroom is
wider than the +38% the door costs in memory.  Neither is the door's
real net: the relative gate caught it, and
tests/test_perf_invariants.py gates it as a COUNT on every platform.
